summary: Instagram is carrying the channel: most Hindi videos get 1,000+ views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly get under 100 views. The best videos are short, surprising 'this thing can't see/think, it only hears/feels' explainers about robots and clap switches, which also earn the most likes, saves and shares. Everyday-object 'how does it know' videos (taps, doors, lifts, smoke alarms) and the English video are getting little attention on either platform.
winningPattern: Robot or hobby-circuit subjects (gyro robot, clap switch, PIR, line follower, IR robot, mic) with a 'X doesn't do Y, it only does Z' contrarian hook in Hinglish, plus an emoji and #shorts. Posted on Instagram Reels first, where they reach 1,000-1,400 people; the ones with a surprising claim or a clear 'why' question get the shares and saves. Early YouTube winners were also in this robot/clap/PIR family and posted around Oct 17-31.
doMore: Make 'it doesn't see/think, it only hears/feels' hooks about robots and maker modules, the top format on both platforms
Do follow-ups to the clap switch and gyro robot videos (a series, e.g. Part 2 with a real build or a failure case) since they are the only ones with real YouTube traction
Open with the surprising claim in the first line on screen and answer the 'why' in the last 3 seconds to boost saves and shares
Stay with Hindi and Hinglish titles for now, and treat Instagram as the main platform while testing what makes YouTube pick videos up
Use hobby/maker subjects (Arduino modules, sensors you can build) over public-place devices, and show a quick build or demo
stopDoing: Stop making generic 'X kaise kaam karta hai?' videos about public devices (mall door, washroom tap, lift, smoke detector); they get under 600 IG views and almost no saves
Stop posting near-duplicate topics (two smoke alarm videos, two IR sensor videos, three tap/door videos) in the same week, as they split attention and none grows
Stop mixing in English videos for now since the one English upload got no Instagram reach
